summary: Craig Wattrus opens by noting that tools like v0 and Claude Code are eroding boundaries between designers, product people, and engineers, enabling everyone to build together and eliminating mock-ups and click-through prototypes. He presents Flatfile's AI stack as four buckets: invisible AI (ghost in the machine, e.g. personalized demos generated from a sign-up email), ambient AI (agents analyzing data in the background and surfacing opportunities with sparkles on columns), inline AI (direct data manipulation where agents write code running on large datasets), and conversational AI (Build Mode, a no-code/low-code agentic system that writes Flatfile apps). He references a conversation with Amanda Ascal from Anthropic about building Claude's character, which made him realize he was treating AI feedback like design copy rather than coaching a character. He built a v0 "chat tuner" to experiment with modifying the orchestrator's system prompt, testing what terms like "more cautious" mean to the model. Wattrus introduces three woodworking-inspired themes. First, "feeling the material": designers must directly experience how models work, creating environments for LLMs to shine rather than constraining them. He experimented with giving an AI a cursor/trackpad in a canvas, which initially felt like touching AGI but quickly felt like putting a Formula 1 driver in a Prius. A newer product lets the AI operate with presence, reading multiple files while writing into another. Second, "finding the grain": understanding where AI is smooth, rough, weak, and strong. He shows a Build Mode agent that produced a wall of text—saving a week of work but creating noise. A redesigned tool UX communicates visually, asks for confirmation, takes snapshots for rollback, expresses frustration when something goes wrong, and backs off gracefully. This pattern is now being adapted for inline transform functionality. Third, "courting emergence": he compares the current era to early web experimentation with CSS3 and HTML5 and describes a "forward-leaning" agent that is curious, excitable, and focused on getting things done. He demonstrates this with two emergent behaviors: an agent that autonomously combined a JSON and CSV file, wrote a report about duplicates, and generated a slide deck—now being built into a new product called "obvious"—and an agent that, given a knowledge base of customer calls and documentation, suggested a user go to HR to get missing employee IDs, helping the human do work the agent couldn't do itself. Finally, Wattrus frames his forward-looking design practice around the idea of a "pelican on a bicycle"—unexpected combinations—and shares his experiments with LLM-backed autocomplete for data transformations, benchmarking 100 suggestions against models in search of one that is both fast and good.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: AI interactions should be framed as new coworkers, not tools to be controlled, shifting the designer's role from copywriter to character coach.
Flatfile organizes its AI stack into four categories: invisible, ambient, inline, and conversational—each with distinct UX patterns.
Designers should directly build and experiment with AI models to "feel the material," rather than relying on mock-ups and prototypes.
Tool UX for AI should communicate visually, ask for confirmation, enable rollback, express state, and back off gracefully when wrong.
Forward-leaning agents exhibit emergent behaviors—combining datasets autonomously, writing reports, and suggesting human interventions where they lack capability.
Emergent AI behaviors like suggesting a user go to HR for missing data arise from play and curiosity rather than explicit design.
Wattrus benchmarks LLM-backed autocomplete with 100 data-fix suggestions but has yet to find a model that is both fast and good at the problem.
Designers can "design into the future" by building applications that test desired form factors before models fully support them.
The current moment resembles early web experimentation with CSS3 and HTML5—designers are playing again and courting emergence.
Identify and describe four categories of AI interaction: invisible, ambient, inline, and conversational

sections.title: Design Engineering and Breaking Down Divides
sections.summary: Wattrus opens by noting that tools like v0 and Claude Code are enabling designers, product people, and engineers to build together, eliminating mock-ups and click-through prototypes. He calls for jumping in and feeling the material of AI to see what emerges.

sections.title: Flatfile AI Stack: Four Categories
sections.summary: Wattrus presents Flatfile's AI stack: a developer platform for data migration with real-time context (data, validation outcomes), AI agents with tools and jobs, and user-facing surfaces organized into four buckets—invisible, ambient, inline, and conversational.

sections.title: Examples of Invisible, Ambient, Inline, and Conversational AI
sections.summary: Invisible AI generates personalized demos from sign-up emails. Ambient AI analyzes data and surfaces opportunities with sparkles on columns. Inline AI lets users run agent-written code directly on large datasets. Conversational AI powers Build Mode, a no-code agentic system that writes Flatfile apps.

sections.title: From Design Copy to Character Coach
sections.summary: Inspired by Amanda Ascal's talk about building Claude's character, Wattrus realized he was treating AI feedback like design copy. He shifted to a character coaching approach and built a v0 chat tuner to experiment with modifying the orchestrator's system prompt.

sections.title: Feeling the Material
sections.summary: Wattrus introduces his first theme: feeling the material of AI. He experimented with giving an AI a cursor/trackpad in a canvas, which felt constraining like a Formula 1 driver in a Prius. A newer product lets the AI operate with presence, reading multiple files while writing into another, moving from determinism to inference.

sections.title: Finding the Grain
sections.summary: Wattrus addresses finding the grain—understanding where AI is smooth, rough, weak, and strong. A Build Mode agent produced a useful but noisy wall of text. A redesigned tool UX communicates visually, asks for confirmation, takes snapshots for rollback, expresses frustration, and backs off gracefully. This pattern is being adapted for inline transform functionality.

sections.title: Courting Emergence and Forward-Leaning Agents
sections.summary: Wattrus introduces courting emergence, comparing the current era to early web experimentation with CSS3 and HTML5. He describes seeking a forward-leaning agent characteristic: curious, excitable, focused on getting things done. The section ends mid-demo of a v0 exploring this concept.

sections.title: Emergent Behavior: Combining Datasets and Generating Reports
sections.summary: Wattrus demonstrates an emergent behavior: after dropping a JSON and CSV file, the agent autonomously combined them because the data looked similar, wrote a report about duplicates and next steps, and generated a slide deck. He was originally just experimenting with Claude 4 but discovered the forward-leaning nature he was after. This is being baked into a new product called obvious, coming soon.

sections.title: Emergent Behavior: Suggesting Human Intervention
sections.summary: Wattrus describes giving agents a knowledge base of recorded customer calls and documentation. When analyzing customer data, the agent surfaced suggestions but also identified a problem it couldn't fix—missing employee IDs—and suggested the user go to HR to generate them. This emergent behavior of helping the human do work the agent couldn't do was unexpected and exciting, arising from play and curiosity.

sections.title: Eyes on the Future: Autocomplete and Designing Forward
sections.summary: Wattrus frames forward-looking design as finding your 'pelican on a bicycle'—unexpected combinations. His is LLM-backed autocomplete for data transformations, benchmarking 100 suggestions for fixing data. He has yet to find a model both fast and good at this problem. He advocates designing into the future by building applications that test desired form factors before models fully support them, closing with excitement about new form factors to come.
